why: The Consent Record is the consent wording EXACTLY AS IT WAS SHOWN, and two
different programs decide what that is: resources/renderer/src/render.ts draws
the sentence in the browser, and src/Lead/ConsentRecord.php composes the
evidence on the server. Neither can defer to the other — the renderer is a
pure function with no server, and the server cannot trust a wording a public
So they are two spellings of one rule, and this file is what stops them
drifting: tests/js/renderer-consent-parity.test.ts renders each node and reads
its text; tests/unit/Lead/ConsentSentenceParityTest.php composes each node and
compares the string. Both assert against `shown`.
The same arrangement the rule and template manifests have (ADR 0005, ADR 0010).
Each case also declares `anchor`: the href the rendered <a> must carry, or null where no anchor renders at all. That is the renderer's half of the same rule — no dead `#`, ever (ADR 0032).

A sentence may also carry %b, filled by `emphasis` and drawn as a <strong>. It takes every rule %s already has — one per sentence, a second is literal, an absent one goes along with the space in front of it — so the cases below are the same cases at a second mark, plus the two where both appear at once.

cases.why: the ordinary case: one placeholder, one resolved link

node.text: I agree to receive emails and accept the %s.

cases.shown: I agree to receive emails and accept the privacy policy.

cases.why: no policy configured: the link renders nothing, and the placeholder goes with it along with the space in front of it (ADR 0032)

node.text: I agree to receive emails and accept the %s.

cases.shown: I agree to receive emails and accept the.

cases.why: no link at all: the placeholder is still not text the visitor read

node.text: I agree to receive emails and accept the %s.

cases.shown: I agree to receive emails and accept the.

cases.why: a link with nowhere to go: no placeholder means no place, so nothing renders
only the FIRST placeholder is a link; a second is literal text, because a sentence carries one link
cases.shown: See the privacy policy, and the %s again.

cases.why: a consent node whose wording nobody has filled in yet — it still enforces, and the evidence says what it says
an href outside the safe schemes: the renderer drops it and renders no anchor, so the evidence must not claim one was there
a link with a resolved href and no label: the anchor renders, empty, so the placeholder is replaced by nothing and the space in front of it stays
emphasis alone: %b is the words, in bold, and the record says them in plain text because that is what was read

node.text: I agree to %b about new arrivals.

cases.shown: I agree to one email a month about new arrivals.

cases.why: both marks, in one sentence: this is why there are two of them rather than one slot with two claimants

node.text: I agree to %b about new arrivals, and accept the %s.

cases.shown: I agree to one email a month about new arrivals, and accept the privacy policy.

cases.why: no emphasis supplied: %b renders nothing and the space in front of it goes too, exactly as an unfilled %s does

node.text: I agree to %b about new arrivals.

cases.shown: I agree to about new arrivals.

cases.why: an empty emphasis is an absent one: there is nothing to set in bold, so no element is built and the mark strips

node.text: I agree to %b about new arrivals.

cases.shown: I agree to about new arrivals.

cases.why: only the FIRST %b is emphasis; a second is literal text, because a sentence carries one run of it

node.text: I agree to %b, and to %b again.

cases.shown: I agree to one email, and to %b again.

cases.why: emphasis with no place to go: no %b means no place, so the words render nowhere rather than glued to the end
